body.text: Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate secures gold mine bowls property even though he was not the proposed buyer
Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate was able to take over from colossal Australian developer Meriton the private purchase of a long-desired slice of prime real estate, the ABC can reveal.

That transfer allowed Mr Tate to purchase a sliver of land to weld with three existing blocks his private entities already co-owned in Surfers Paradise. The four-term politician and partners then flipped those combined properties in a $33 million site deal.

The mayor and Meriton, which has multiple Gold Coast projects, declined to answer questions including what the politician's private company paid for the development company's option rights for the land.
"The matters raised relate to private commercial matters," the mayor's office told the ABC.
Mr Tate's property acquisition last year had previously created controversy.
But Meriton's involvement has not previously been reported, while the seller says he had not planned on the mayor being the acquirer.
About 600 metres from golden beaches and five minutes' walk from Cavill Avenue's glitz, the former bowls club land is now prime real estate in Australia's sixth-biggest city.
Mr Tate, 67, promotes the city as "open for business" and has a headline-grabbing profile, even last month winning a Masters Pan Pacific powerlifting title.
He has retained development interests, with the mayor's property business touting plans 13 years ago for a 389-unit residential tower and 216-apartment hotel on that site.
Court and land records show a property group associated with Mr Tate, who entered politics in 2012, acquired two blocks there in 2007 for $770,000, and another for almost $2.3 million in 2016.
But council owned a final fourth block needed to complete a development site.
In 2022, that fourth block went up for public tender, and a Turner Family Properties subsidiary acquired it for $1.785 million.

The company's Peter Turner appeared on the newly bought land in a social media post. "With over 90m frontage to the Gold Coast Highway, and unlimited height zoning, we are excited," the company posted.
The family business had floated building a medical centre, although questions remained about property access that Mr Turner maintained he could secure.
In early 2025, real estate agent Roland Evans approached. He told the ABC that developer Meriton had considered acquiring the Turner land and the other three blocks linked to Mr Tate.
Documents seen by the ABC show an initial offer stated Meriton or a fully owned subsidiary acting as a nominee would acquire that Turner family company-owned land.

Around April 2025, the Turner subsidiary and a Meriton subsidiary signed an option contract to buy the land for $3.8 million excluding GST. But contract conditions included that Meriton subsidiary could nominate someone else to acquire the land.
Mr Evans, who a year later attended a controversial Mar-a-Lago dinner involving Mr Tate and US president Donald Trump, said this was a normal contract condition of which the seller was aware.
Within months, Meriton transferred its purchasing right to the company Crestden, of which Mr Tate is director and owns half the shares.

Meriton told the ABC it conducted due diligence before ultimately deciding against acquiring "the site for commercial reasons". Meriton would "not comment on the commercial terms of individual transactions".

Property records show Meriton's subsidiary temporarily took a caveat against that Turner family block during the option period but did not secure one against the other three blocks linked to Mr Tate's company.

A 60-year Australian development stalwart, Meriton has built more than 80,000 apartments. Its current Cypress Palms project in Surfers Paradise includes a 90-storey tower while three-bedroom apartments start at $1.505 million.
Mr Tate awarded keys to the city in 2024 to Meriton's legendary founder Harry Triguboff. The mayor and other councillors all voted for a Meriton project that year too.
But the land seller in the 2025 transfer of the land-purchase option to Mr Tate's company indicated they were upset.
Mr Turner said they would have sought a higher price if they had known Mr Tate's company would end up buying.
"It was worth more to Tom Tate than anyone else in the world," Mr Turner told the ABC.
Mr Turner said while they could have tried rejecting the sale, it ultimately proceeded after receiving advice to just take the offer and about any potential sale dispute dragging out.
A separate spat has emerged though about a real estate commission, with Mr Evans saying he was still seeking it from the Turner family company.
Mr Evans said he believed Meriton had genuinely planned to acquire the land, spending an "awful lot of money doing their due diligence (before) they transferred the option".

After Mr Tate's company acquired the final land sliver in July last year, he and partner companies sold all four blocks as a site. A subsidiary of AW Holding Group, developer of the Gold Coast's Jewel residences, acquired that site for $33 million in November 2025.
Mr Tate's company and those partners had paid more than $7 million acquiring blocks since 2007, according to records.

The mayor's involvement resurfaced after the politician in May last year recused himself when a majority of council rejected a proposed concrete batching project, near Burleigh, owned by the Turner family.

The mayor said then a "third party" was eyeing his Surfers Paradise land and the adjoining block of "Peter Turner", and while he did not believe a conflict of interest existed he would recuse himself.

But this August, with the land acquisition finished, the mayor voted for adopting a new council-staff recommendation about the concrete project. Court documents show council has agreed to drop opposition, subject to conditions, so ending a planning appeal from the Turner family business.

The mayor declined to say why he decided to vote this time, citing the appeal. Asked about handling any future Meriton projects before council, his office said Mr Tate "observes all applicable conflict of interest disclosure requirements".
Meriton said any council deals were conducted "at arms-length and through the standard planning process".
